claims.text: A context map pictures the bounded contexts and how each pair depends on the other; the upstream context is the one whose model the other depends on, the downstream one adapts when that model changes; changes travel upstream to downstream, not the reverse.
claims.source_hint: Domain-Driven Design (Evans), Maintaining Model Integrity: Context Map; upstream/downstream relationships

claims.text: Context Map, upstream and downstream context are terms from Evans' Domain-Driven Design (strategic design).

claims.text: At stage-2 Program.cs sets options.MapInboundClaims = false and TokenValidationParameters.RoleClaimType = "roles" (lines 52-55); with MapInboundClaims false, JwtBearer keeps incoming claim names (sub, roles) as written in the token instead of mapping them to long ClaimTypes URIs.

claims.text: With RoleClaimType = "roles", role checks (RequireRole("staff") in the StaffOnly policy, IsInRole("staff") in OrderOwnerHandler) read only the roles claim; a token without that claim is in no role, so staff are refused on StaffOnly endpoints while the build still passes.

claims.text: At stage-2 OrderOwnerHandler reads the caller's sub with context.User.FindFirstValue("sub") and looks the customer up with FindByIdentitySubjectAsync.

At stage-2 each Notification row is one email to send (Entities.cs:117-118); NotificationSender.SendOneAsync (65-81) reads notification.Order!.Customer! (69) and the Customer's Email and FullName (70-71); renaming Customer.FullName makes NotificationSender.cs fail to compile.
At stage-2 NotificationSender is a hosted service in the DonHang.Api process (AddHostedService in Program.cs), so ordering and notifications run in one process with no network call between them.
AddJwtBearer fetches Keycloak's metadata and signing keys and checks each token itself, without calling Keycloak on every request.

claims.text: refund-design.md: step 4 sends a key so a resend does not refund twice; step 6 records the gateway's confirmation. Open questions: if the gateway ignores keys, step 4 must ask refund status before each resend (R2); if it reports only by calling back, step 6 must change (R1).
At stage-1 Đơn Hàng signed people in itself (AuthController, PasswordHasher); stage-2 removed that code and hands sign-in to Keycloak.
Upstream/downstream is decided by whose model is followed, not by who sends requests: the API requests Keycloak's keys yet Keycloak is upstream; a gateway that called back would still be upstream.

Being downstream is the usual price of reusing others' work, not a mistake; when a generic subdomain is reused, following its model is part of the choice, and the map's value is that the dependency is written down.

refund-design.md step 3 runs a job the same way as NotificationSender (2 s tick, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED); step 5 sets its own retry (1, 2, 4, 8 min, at most 1 h apart, within 24 h), unlike NotificationSender's 2, 4, 8, 16 s and 5 attempts.
Where a break shows first depends on how the downstream side holds the upstream model (text checked at run time, compiled classes, a plan); summarises claims 4, 7 and 10.

Stage-2's one API holds several bounded contexts: ordering, the product catalogue and notifications (Order.Status vs Notification.Status words). NotificationSender is a hosted job with no caller and reads no token claims.
